Comment:
>>254912782
>i'm not really trying to push my preconceptions here

Don't worry mate, no one is slinging mud at you quite yet. (Or 'throwing the first stone', lol.)

>my point is that we need to know who or what we're dealing with if we want to plan for long term

No one is really planning for the long term. It is folly to believe that the long term can be planned for. Please see >>254909055 for more on this, Ted has addressed this matter in ISAIF. 

>Or do you guys believe this is our first run at a hypertech race?

Building on what is stated here, >>254909055 , whether or not this has happened in the past is completely irrelevant to the reality of the problem at hand TODAY. What matters is that it is happening NOW, to us. 'The world belongs to the living', wrote Jünger in his WWI diary. He was right. 

>is it a universal agent? Like nature itself is a technological dead end until we are much more evolved as a species? or are we dealing with gatekeepers

Who knows...? Maybe it is a universal agent, after all, the laws of physics, logic, etc. seem constant and immutable enough to infer universality.... And if someone DOES truly know about some non-organic intelligence behind all of this, how do they even prove it to the rest of the world...? It is sufficiently clear though that technological progress WILL eventually lead to the obliteration of the human mammal. That fact ALONE should be enough to take matters seriously. 

You really should consider reading Ellul's 'La Technique ou l'enjeu du siècle'. He will show you how irrelevant any 'religious/spiritual' overtones are to the actual problem; and all of this taking into account that Ellul himself was a faithful Christian.... Plus, if you really are française as your flag suggests, you can read him in the original language, instead of some fucking translation.... nothing to lose, anon. 

Thank you for expanding/clarifying on your previous posts.

>I think I understand Ted better now. He didn’t have the time or wish to plan for an ideal society, whether it had tech or not, just that the current system needs to be destroyed. What would come later? That will be decided later. Wise man.

Ted directly addressed the point you make here:

From ISAIF:

182. It will be objected that the French and Russian Revolutions were failures. But most revolutions have two goals. One is to destroy an old form of society and the other is to set up the new form of society envisioned by the revolutionaries. The French and Russian revolutionaries failed (fortunately!) to create the new kind of society of which they dreamed, but they were quite successful in destroying the old society. We have no illusions about the feasibility of creating a new, ideal form of society. Our goal is only to destroy the existing form of society."}]
